title: Поступок настоящего мужчины  (The Act of a Real Man)

segments.t: After Katya flees in tears, Eleonora emerges from the bathroom and tells Denis he acted like a real man by taking the blame on himself. Downstairs, Barinov comforts his heartbroken daughter while Denis wonders if he can still make things right.
Ты поступил как мужчина.
Спасибо тебе за молчание.
Бывают моменты, когда мы отчаянно злимся на самих себя из-за поступков,
которые мы совершили.
Из-за людей, которые счастливы без нас.
Катя, дочка моя!
Ты опять, да?
Катя? Опять?
Папа, мне очень плохо.
Из-за слов, которые сказали, не подумав.
Может, пора перестать себя ненавидеть и попытаться что-то исправить?
Хотя бы попытаться.
Now let's go back through their conversation line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
Ты поступил как мужчина.
'You acted like a man.' Eleonora favors an emphatic tone during the exchange, joining "postupil" ("acted") to "kak" ("how") so every word pulls its weight.
Спасибо тебе за молчание.
'Thank you for keeping silent.' Eleonora presents an honest tone in this beat, putting "spasibo" ("thank you") alongside "molchaniye" ("silence") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.

'that we committed.' Denis picks a natural mood without hesitation, leaning on "sovershili" ("accomplished") before closing the thought with "kotoryye" ("which, that").

'Because of the people who are happy without us.' Denis brings an unhurried view as they talk, putting "lyudey" ("people") alongside "schastlivy" ("happy") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
Катя, дочка моя!
'Katya, my daughter!' Barinov chooses a brisk course in the room, putting "dochka" ("dear, daughter") alongside "katya" ("Katya") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
Ты опять, да?
'You are drinking again, huh?' Barinov inquires honestly right away, joining "opyat" ("again") to "ty" ("you") so every word pulls its weight.
Катя? Опять?
'Katya? Again?' Barinov probes briskly on the spot, pairing "opyat" ("again") with "katya" ("Katya") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
Папа, мне очень плохо.
'Dad, I feel terrible.' Barinov favors a natural course as the scene unfolds, weaving "papa" ("Dad") together with "ochen" ("very much") just the way native speakers do.
Из-за слов, которые сказали, не подумав.
'Because of the words we spoke without thinking.' Denis strikes a brisk tempo with Eleonora, weaving "slov" ("words") together with "skazali" ("told") just the way native speakers do.
Может, пора перестать себя ненавидеть и попытаться что-то исправить?
'Maybe it is time to stop hating ourselves and try to fix something?' Denis presses promptly during the talk, combining "mozhet" ("can") and "pora" ("it's time") so the key meaning lands right away.
Хотя бы попытаться.
'At least try.' Denis favors an easygoing note for Eleonora, leaning on "popytatsya" ("to try, attempt") before closing the thought with "khotya" ("at least").
